title: Section 1.4: Multiplying Polynomials & The FOIL Strategy
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 08 • Section 1.4 (Workbook p. 14)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### The FOIL Method for Multiplying Two Binomials
$$(a + b)(c + d) = \underbrace{ac}_{\text{First}} + \underbrace{ad}_{\text{Outer}} + \underbrace{bc}_{\text{Inner}} + \underbrace{bd}_{\text{Last}}$$
- **Every term in the first polynomial** must multiply **every term in the second polynomial**.
- Combine like terms (typically the Outer and Inner products).
pitfall: **Sora's Warning:** FOIL is just a memory aid for the distributive property. When multiplying a binomial by a trinomial, FOIL expands to 6 multiplications!
script:
[Prof. Park] Welcome everyone to Lecture 08 of M090 Introductory Algebra! I am Professor Eunju Park, and joining me is TA Sora. Today, we explore Section 1.4 of our course workbook, spanning pages 14 and 15: Multiplying Polynomials and the FOIL Strategy. Hello everyone!

[TA Sora] Today we learn how to multiply binomials and polynomials together. This is one of the most famous and heavily used procedures in all of secondary and college mathematics.

[Prof. Park] Whether you are finding the area of a newly planned building footprint in Bozeman, calculating economic revenue functions (price times quantity) for a business in Belgrade, or factoring quadratic equations in Unit 2, polynomial multiplication is the universal engine behind it all. That is right, Sora.

[TA Sora] When we multiply two binomialsâlike (a + b)(c + d)âevery term in the first binomial must multiply every term in the second binomial. To help students remember all four multiplications without missing any, educators developed the famous acronym: FOIL! F stands for First terms. O stands for Outer terms.

[Prof. Park] I stands for Inner terms. L stands for Last terms. You can also think of FOIL geometrically as an area model or a 2-by-2 Punnett square: draw a rectangle partitioned into 4 smaller cells. The top sides are a and b, and the left sides are c and d.

[TA Sora] The areas of the four cells are ac, ad, bc, and bd! When you sum the cells together, you get the exact same result. Visual learners in architectural drafting and carpentry often love the box model, while algebraic thinkers love the rhythmic flow of FOIL.

[Prof. Park] Let's examine how the FOIL strategy works on slide 2 with Example 1! Imagine you are designing a high-performance energy-efficient modular home for a client building in the Bridger Foothills.

[TA Sora] If one room module has length (2x + 5) feet and width (3x - 4) feet, calculating the total square footage requires finding the product of those two binomials. Every square foot of flooring, insulation, and solar radiant heating depends on correctly multiplying these algebraic dimensions!

[Prof. Park] That is why polynomial multiplication is not an abstract puzzleâit is physical reality in construction and architecture.

title: Example 1A & 1B: Standard FOIL Binomial Multiplication
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 08 • Section 1.4 Example 1A & 1B (Workbook p. 14)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Use the distributive property to multiply and fully simplify (Workbook p. 14)
$$\text{A. } (2x + 4)(3x + 5)$$
$$\text{B. } (x - 4)(5x - 1)$$
pitfall: **Double Negative Trap:** In 1B, Last times Last is $(-4)(-1) = +4$. Watch your signs!
script:
[Prof. Park] Let's examine Section 1.4 Examples 1A and 1B on workbook page 14: Part A: (2x + 4)(3x + 5). Part B: (x - 6)(x + 8).

[TA Sora] Let's execute FOIL step by step on Part A: (2x + 4)(3x + 5): F - First terms: multiply the first terms of each binomial: (2x)(3x) = 6x^2. O - Outer terms: multiply the terms on the far outside: (2x)(5) = +10x.

[Prof. Park] I - Inner terms: multiply the terms on the inside: (4)(3x) = +12x. L - Last terms: multiply the last terms of each binomial: (4)(5) = +20. Now write all four products in a line: 6x^2 + 10x + 12x + 20.

[TA Sora] Notice that the two middle termsâthe Outer and Inner termsâare like terms! Both have x to the first power. 10x + 12x = 22x. Combining them gives our final trinomial: 6x^2 + 22x + 20! Now let's tackle Part B: (x - 6)(x + 8). Watch your signs carefully here!

[Prof. Park] F - First: (x)(x) = x^2. O - Outer: (x)(8) = +8x. I - Inner: (-6)(x) = -6x. L - Last: (-6)(8) = -48. Combine the middle like terms: +8x - 6x = +2x. Our final trinomial is: x^2 + 2x - 48.

[TA Sora] Notice the predictable rhythm: First gives the quadratic term, Outer and Inner combine to give the linear term, and Last gives the constant. If you do this 5 times, your hand will automatically glide through FOIL without even pausing to think.

[Prof. Park] You can also visualize monomial multiplication as distributing paint across a series of connected rectangular rooms. That is a wonderful visual! 3x^2 is the height of the wall, and (4x^3 - 5x + 7) is the broken-up length of three adjoining rooms.

[TA Sora] The total area is the sum of the three individual room areas: 12x^5 - 15x^3 + 21x^2!

title: Example 1C & 1D: Binomial Products with Leading Constants
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 08 • Section 1.4 Example 1C & 1D (Workbook p. 14)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Use the distributive property to multiply and fully simplify (Workbook p. 14)
$$\text{C. } 2(b - 3)(b + 4)$$
$$\text{D. } 4(w + 2)(w - 2)$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ C:}\quad & \text{Step 1: FOIL the binomials first:} \\
& (b - 3)(b + 4) = b^2 + 4b - 3b - 12 = b^2 + b - 12 \\
& \text{Step 2: Distribute the outer 2:} \\
& 2(b^2 + b - 12) = \mathbf{2b^2 + 2b - 24} \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ D:}\quad & \text{Step 1: Difference of squares for } (w + 2)(w - 2): \\
& w^2 - 2w + 2w - 4 = w^2 - 4 \\
& \text{Step 2: Distribute the outer 4:} \\
& 4(w^2 - 4) = \mathbf{4w^2 - 16}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Sora's Strategy:** FOIL the binomials inside parentheses first, and distribute the constant factor last! Never distribute the constant into BOTH parentheses!
script:
[Prof. Park] Now look at slide 3 with Examples 1C and 1D: Binomial Products with Leading Constants: Part C: 2(b - 3)(b + 4). Part D: -3(2y - 1)(3y + 4). In Part C, we have three factors: the constant 2, and two binomials (b - 3) and (b + 4).

[TA Sora] Students often ask: 'Should I distribute the 2 first, or FOIL the binomials first?' And more dangerously, some students distribute the 2 to BOTH binomialsâwriting (2b - 6)(2b + 8)! That is completely wrongâthat would be multiplying by 4, not 2! Multiplication is associative, so 2 multiplies only once.

[Prof. Park] That is such a vital distinction, Sora. Sora's Golden Tip is: FOIL the binomials first, keep them inside protective parentheses, and distribute the leading constant at the very end! Let's follow that advice for Part C: FOIL (b - 3)(b + 4): First: b Â· b = b^2.

[TA Sora] Outer: b Â· 4 = +4b. Inner: -3 Â· b = -3b. Last: -3 Â· 4 = -12. Combine middle terms: 4b - 3b = +b. So the binomial product is (b^2 + b - 12).

[Prof. Park] Now multiply the entire trinomial by the leading 2: 2(b^2 + b - 12) = 2b^2 + 2b - 24! Look how effortless that was! Now look at Part D: -3(2y - 1)(3y + 4). FOIL the binomials first: First: (2y)(3y) = 6y^2. Outer: (2y)(4) = +8y.

[TA Sora] Inner: (-1)(3y) = -3y. Last: (-1)(4) = -4. Combine middle terms: 8y - 3y = +5y, giving (6y^2 + 5y - 4). Now distribute the leading -3: (-3)(6y^2) = -18y^2. (-3)(+5y) = -15y. (-3)(-4) = +12. Final result: -18y^2 - 15y + 12. Methodical execution produces effortless accuracy.

[Prof. Park] Here is a memory hook for FOIL: First, Outer, Inner, Last. Notice that Outer and Inner are the 'middle children' of the problemâthey almost always share the exact same variable power and combine together into a single middle term!

[TA Sora] But always be cautious with your signs: if the outer product is negative and the inner product is positive, you must add integers carefully: -10x + 12x = +2x.

title: Example 1E & 1F: Squaring a Binomial Trap
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 08 • Section 1.4 Example 1E & 1F (Workbook p. 14)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ E:}\quad & \text{Write out as repeated multiplication:} \\
& (2y - 7)(2y - 7) = (2y)(2y) + (2y)(-7) + (-7)(2y) + (-7)(-7) \\
&= 4y^2 - 14y - 14y + 49 = \mathbf{4y^2 - 28y + 49} \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ F:}\quad & \text{Expand } (y - 7)^2 \text{ first:} \\
& (y - 7)(y - 7) = y^2 - 14y + 49 \\
& \text{Now multiply by 2:} \\
& 2(y^2 - 14y + 49) = \mathbf{2y^2 - 28y + 98}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **THE DEADLIEST ALGEBRA SIN:** $(2y - 7)^2 \neq 4y^2 + 49$! Exponents DO NOT distribute over subtraction! You MUST write it twice and FOIL to get the middle term $-28y$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 4 highlights the single most notorious trap in introductory algebra: Squaring a Binomial! Part E: (2y - 7)^2. Part F: 2(y - 7)^2. Sora, sound the alarm! MAXIMUM ALERT LEVEL! (2y - 7)^2 does NOT equal (2y)^2 - 7^2!

[TA Sora] Students who distribute the exponent 2 get 4y^2 - 49 or 4y^2 + 49, and they lose all points on the problem! Exponents do NOT distribute across addition or subtraction! Think geometrically: if you have a square of side (a + b), its area is (a + b)^2.

[Prof. Park] That large square contains a square of size a^2, a square of size b^2, AND two large rectangles of size a Â· b! If you write a^2 + b^2, you threw away both rectangles! That is like buying a house and forgetting the living room!

[TA Sora] That is a wonderful mental visual! Squaring a binomial means multiplying that entire binomial by ITSELF! Whenever you see (2y - 7)^2, immediately write it as two side-by-side parentheses: (2y - 7)(2y - 7)! Now FOIL: First: (2y)(2y) = 4y^2. Outer: (2y)(-7) = -14y. Inner: (-7)(2y) = -14y.

[Prof. Park] Last: (-7)(-7) = +49. Now look at the middle terms: -14y and -14y do NOT cancel! They ADD: -14y - 14y = -28y! So (2y - 7)^2 = 4y^2 - 28y + 49. The middle term -28y is essential! And look at Part F: 2(y - 7)^2.

[TA Sora] First write (y - 7)^2 as (y - 7)(y - 7). FOIL gives: y^2 - 7y - 7y + 49 = y^2 - 14y + 49. Now distribute the leading 2: 2(y^2 - 14y + 49) = 2y^2 - 28y + 98.

[Prof. Park] Write out both binomials every time, and you will never drop the middle term. Let us draw the geometric area model for (3x + 4)^2: draw a large square of side length 3x + 4. Split each side into two segments: 3x and 4.

[TA Sora] That divides the large square into FOUR distinct rooms! One room is 3x by 3x = 9x^2. One room is 4 by 4 = 16. And there are TWO identical hallway rooms, each measuring 3x by 4 = 12x! The two hallway rooms together give 12x + 12x = 24x!

[Prof. Park] If you forget the middle term, you are literally erasing two whole rooms from your house blueprint!

title: Example 1H & 1I: Multiplying Binomials by Trinomials
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 08 • Section 1.4 Example 1H & 1I (Workbook p. 14)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Multiply and combine like terms (Workbook p. 14)
$$\text{H. } (w + 2)(w^2 - 2w + 9)$$
$$\text{I. } (2x - 1)(x^2 + 3x - 10)$$
pitfall: **Notice Quadratic Cancellation:** In Part H, $-2w^2 + 2w^2 = 0$. The $w^2$ terms completely vanish!
script:
[Prof. Park] Let's expand our horizons on slide 5 with Examples 1H and 1I: Multiplying Binomials by Trinomials: Part H: (w + 2)(w^2 - 2w + 9). Part I: (2x - 3)(x^2 + 4x - 5).

[TA Sora] When multiplying a 2-term binomial by a 3-term trinomial, FOIL expands into the generalized distributive property: Each of the 2 terms in the first group must multiply each of the 3 terms in the second group. 2 times 3 equals 6 total multiplications!

[Prof. Park] Let's do Part H systematically: First, distribute w to all three terms: w(w^2) = w^3. w(-2w) = -2w^2. w(9) = +9w. Next, distribute +2 to all three terms: 2(w^2) = +2w^2. 2(-2w) = -4w. 2(9) = +18. Now align like terms: w^3 is alone.

[TA Sora] Quadratic terms: -2w^2 + 2w^2 = 0w^2! They cancel completely! Linear terms: +9w - 4w = +5w. Constant: +18. Our final result is: w^3 + 5w + 18! Now let's tackle Part I: (2x - 3)(x^2 + 4x - 5).

[Prof. Park] Distribute 2x to all three terms: (2x)(x^2) = 2x^3. (2x)(4x) = +8x^2. (2x)(-5) = -10x. Now distribute -3 to all three terms: (-3)(x^2) = -3x^2. (-3)(4x) = -12x. (-3)(-5) = +15. Now combine like terms: Cubic: 2x^3. Quadratic: 8x^2 - 3x^2 = +5x^2. Linear: -10x - 12x = -22x.

[TA Sora] Constant: +15. Final polynomial: 2x^3 + 5x^2 - 22x + 15! Six multiplications combined into four clean terms. Notice why difference of squares is so unique: because the two middle terms are exact opposites (+35x and -35x), they cancel each other out completely!

[Prof. Park] It is like paying 35 dollars and immediately receiving 35 dollars backâyour net change is zero! That leaves only the square of the first term minus the square of the second term: 25x^2 - 49.

[TA Sora] Whenever you see conjugate binomials (A - B)(A + B), you can instantly write down A^2 - B^2!

title: Example 2 & 3: Perimeter & Area Applications
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 08 • Section 1.4 Example 2 & 3 (Workbook p. 15)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Geometry Applications of Polynomials (Workbook p. 15)
A rectangle has length $L = 3x - 4$ and width $W = 2x + 7$.
- **Example 2:** Find the perimeter of the rectangle.
- **Example 3:** Find the area of the rectangle.
pitfall: **Don't Mix Up Perimeter & Area:** Perimeter adds all 4 sides ($2L + 2W$, linear units). Area multiplies length by width ($L \cdot W$, square units)!
script:
[Prof. Park] Moving to slide 6, let's examine Examples 2 and 3: Real-World Geometry Applications on workbook page 15. A rectangle has length L = 3x - 4 and width W = 2x + 1. Example 2 asks for the Perimeter. Example 3 asks for the Area.

[TA Sora] This is where algebra directly connects to physical space and cost estimating! In Gallatin County construction, if a general contractor is installing baseboard trim around the room, they need the Perimeter. If they are ordering hardwood flooring planks, they need the Area!

[Prof. Park] For Perimeter, the distance all the way around a rectangle is: P = 2L + 2W. Substitute our algebraic expressions: P = 2(3x - 4) + 2(2x + 1). Distribute: 2(3x) - 2(4) = 6x - 8. And 2(2x) + 2(1) = 4x + 2.

[TA Sora] Combine like terms: 6x + 4x = 10x, and -8 + 2 = -6. So Perimeter P = 10x - 6 linear units! Now Example 3 asks for the Area. The area of a rectangle is length times width: A = L Â· W.

[Prof. Park] So we must multiply the two binomials: A = (3x - 4)(2x + 1)! This is a job for FOIL: First: (3x)(2x) = 6x^2. Outer: (3x)(1) = +3x. Inner: (-4)(2x) = -8x. Last: (-4)(1) = -4. Combine middle terms: 3x - 8x = -5x.

[TA Sora] So Area A = 6x^2 - 5x - 4 square units! Notice the clear distinction: Perimeter is an addition problem of degree 1 (10x - 6), while Area is a multiplication problem of degree 2 (6x^2 - 5x - 4). The mathematical degree matches the physical dimensions!

[Prof. Park] When multiplying a binomial by a trinomial, I strongly recommend writing your work in a 2-by-3 grid or lining up like terms vertically:
Row 1 from distributing 2x: 2x^3 + 8x^2 - 10x. Row 2 from distributing -3:       - 3x^2 - 12x + 15.

[TA Sora] Lining up the x^2 and x terms vertically makes combining them practically foolproof! Vertical alignment prevents students from skipping terms or accidentally combining unlike powers. Neatness on paper translates directly into 100% test scores!

title: Example 4: Modified Geometric Area Problem
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 08 • Section 1.4 Example 4 (Workbook p. 15)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Modified Rectangle Dimensions (Workbook p. 15)
A given rectangle has length $2x + 3$ and width $x - 6$.
If the **length is decreased by 7** and the **width is increased by 12**, find the **area of the new rectangle** in terms of $x$.
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Step 1: } & \text{Find new dimensions:} \\
& L_{\text{new}} = (2x + 3) - 7 = \mathbf{2x - 4} \\
& W_{\text{new}} = (x - 6) + 12 = \mathbf{x + 6} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 2: } & \text{Calculate new area: } A_{\text{new}} = L_{\text{new}} \cdot W_{\text{new}} \\
& A_{\text{new}} = (2x - 4)(x + 6) \\
&= 2x(x) + 2x(6) - 4(x) - 4(6) \\
&= 2x^2 + 12x - 4x - 24 = \mathbf{2x^2 + 8x - 24}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Sora's Check:** Update BOTH dimensions before multiplying! $(2x - 4)(x + 6)$, then FOIL to get $2x^2 + 8x - 24$!
script:
[Prof. Park] To conclude Lecture 08, let's examine Example 4 on slide 7: Modified Rectangle Dimensions on workbook page 15. A given rectangle has length 2x + 3 and width x - 6.

[TA Sora] If the length is increased by 4 and the width is decreased by 2, find the simplified polynomial expression for the new area. Let's adjust the dimensions first: Original Length = 2x + 3. Increased by 4: (2x + 3) + 4 = 2x + 7.

[Prof. Park] Original Width = x - 6. Decreased by 2: (x - 6) - 2 = x - 8. Now our new dimensions are Length = 2x + 7 and Width = x - 8!

[TA Sora] Now find the new area by multiplying the modified binomials: Area = (2x + 7)(x - 8). Execute FOIL: First: (2x)(x) = 2x^2. Outer: (2x)(-8) = -16x. Inner: (7)(x) = +7x. Last: (7)(-8) = -56. Combine the middle like terms: -16x + 7x = -9x.

[Prof. Park] Our new area is: 2x^2 - 9x - 56 square units! Let's do a quick reality check: suppose x = 10 feet. Original dimensions would be 2(10)+3 = 23 ft by 10-6 = 4 ft, area = 92 sq ft.

[TA Sora] New dimensions: 2(10)+7 = 27 ft by 10-8 = 2 ft, area = 54 sq ft. Now test our algebraic formula: 2(10)^2 - 9(10) - 56 = 2(100) - 90 - 56 = 200 - 146 = 54 sq ft! It matches with 100% precision.

[Prof. Park] In Lecture 09, we transition to Section 1.5 on workbook page 16: Adding and Subtracting Rational Expressions. We will apply our fraction arithmetic from Lecture 01 to algebraic fractions with variables in the denominators. Fantastic work today, everyone, and we will see you in Lecture 09!

[TA Sora] And here is a secret preview: in Chapter 2, we will do this exact process in REVERSE! Reversing multiplication is called FACTORING! If you master FOIL and distribution today, factoring next week will feel completely natural and intuitive. Excellent work mastering polynomial multiplication!
